title.en: RoPE Frequencies: Every Dimension Pair Gets Its Own Clock

description.en: Rotary Position Embeddings don't add a position vector to the token embedding -- they rotate it. Each pair of dimensions inside a head rotates at its own fixed frequency. Compute those frequencies and the resulting rotation angles for a real Llama-shaped head_dim=128 config.

story_variants.en:
## Position by Rotation, Not by Addition

"`positional_encoding` taught you the classic trick: add a sinusoidal vector to the token embedding before attention even starts," Vaathiyaar says. "RoPE -- Rotary Position Embeddings -- does something different. It doesn't touch the embedding at all. Instead, right before the query and key vectors are dot-producted inside attention, RoPE *rotates* each one by an angle that depends on its position in the sequence. Llama, Qwen, Mistral -- every model in the `gqa_kv_head_grouping` lesson's list uses RoPE for exactly this."

### Dimensions Come in Pairs

A query or key vector has `head_dim` numbers in it -- 128 for a Llama-3-8B-shaped head. RoPE splits those 128 numbers into 64 **pairs**, and rotates every pair by its own angle, like 64 independent clock hands living inside one vector. Pair `i` (there are `head_dim / 2` of them, indexed `0` to `63`) gets a fixed frequency:

```
theta_i = base ** (-(2 * i) / head_dim)
```

with `base = 10000` by default (the same constant appears in Llama, Qwen, and Mistral configs as `rope_theta`).

### Fast Pairs, Slow Pairs

Pair `0` gets `theta_0 = base ** 0 = 1.0` -- the fastest clock, rotating a full `1.0` radian for every single position step. Pair `32` -- the midpoint of 64 pairs -- gets `theta_32 = base ** -0.5 = 0.01`, a hundred times slower. Pair `63`, the slowest, barely moves at all per step. The **rotation angle** for pair `i` at sequence position `pos` is just `pos * theta_i`: how far that pair's clock hand has swung by the time you reach that position.

> **Vaathiyaar's rule:** low-index pairs are fast clocks that tell attention about *nearby* positions precisely; high-index pairs are slow clocks that only start to distinguish *far apart* positions. Stacking 64 clocks running at 64 different speeds is what lets one rotation encode position at every distance scale at once.

Today you compute both: the frequency `theta_i` for a given pair, and the rotation angle at a given position.

under_the_hood.summary: RoPE splits each query and key head vector into pairs of numbers and rotates pair i by the angle position x theta_i, where theta_i = base^(-2i / head_dim); low pairs rotate fast and high pairs rotate slowly, like clock hands at different speeds.

steps.title: Rotate, do not add
steps.body: Classic positional encoding adds a vector to the embedding once. RoPE leaves embeddings alone and, inside every attention layer, rotates the query and key vectors by an angle that depends on their position, just before the dot product.

steps.title: Pairs of dimensions
steps.body: A head vector of head_dim = 128 numbers is treated as 64 two-dimensional pairs. Each pair is rotated like a point on a plane by its own angle.

steps.title: Each pair has its own frequency
steps.body: theta_i = base^(-2i / head_dim) with base = 10000. Pair 0 has theta = 1.0 radian per position, pair 32 has 0.01, pair 63 about 0.000115.

steps.title: Angle grows with position
steps.body: At position pos, pair i is rotated by pos x theta_i. Pair 0 swings 1 radian per token, so it distinguishes nearby tokens; pair 63 barely moves over thousands of tokens, so it tracks coarse, long-range position.

steps.title: Same frequencies, every layer and head
steps.body: The rotation has no learned parameters; the frequencies are fixed by base and head_dim. Llama, Qwen and Mistral all use this scheme, differing mainly in the base value.

under_the_hood.takeaway: RoPE encodes position as rotation, with a spectrum of speeds across dimension pairs. Fast pairs resolve fine position; slow pairs cover long distances.
